title: How HTTPS Keeps Your Data Private
performance: After the lesson the viewer explains in their own words why a padlocked site protects what they send (identity check, shared key, scrambled data), and before typing something sensitive reads the site name exactly and looks for a certificate warning, knowing the padlock does not vouch for the site's owner.

audience.assumed_prior: Uses browsers daily, has seen the padlock, knows little or nothing about how it works. No jargon assumed.
audience.why: Corporate employees across functions; prior knowledge is the only attribute worth branching on, so the lesson starts from the padlock they already see.
audience.motivation: Wants to know whether what they type at work and at home can be read by anyone else.
audience.context: A short two minute video watched at a desk; they need one habit they can use the same day.

strategy.name: scenario_led
strategy.rationale: One form submission with one watcher on the path runs through hook, build, check and payoff, so each idea is met as the next thing that happens to the same request. Fits a conceptual topic with no numbers and a short length for practitioners who want decisions soon.
strategy.signature_move: Send one form submission along the path; change the watcher's view at each step: readable, identity checked, key agreed, scrambled; then test the same request on a failed check.

misconceptions.belief: Nobody but the browser and the server can get at what I send; the network between them is private.
misconceptions.why_tempting: Nothing visible happens on the way, and most people on a path never look, so it feels private.
misconceptions.evidence: F1, F2: plain traffic is readable text and crosses devices such as Wi-Fi access points and routers; anyone who controls or taps one can copy it. Say 'can', not 'does'.

misconceptions.belief: If the padlock is showing, the site is safe and its owner can be trusted.
misconceptions.why_tempting: A padlock looks like a seal of approval.
misconceptions.evidence: F14, F15: the padlock means the connection is encrypted and the certificate matched the site name; a bad actor can hold a valid certificate for their own name.

misconceptions.belief: The padlock protects my data wherever it goes, including after it arrives.
misconceptions.why_tempting: 'Secure' sounds like it covers the whole journey and what happens after.
misconceptions.evidence: F16: the server's owner receives the data in readable form and can store or misuse it.

hook.sketch: Imagine you press Submit on a login form while a watcher sits on the path. What does the watcher see?
hook.on_screen_essence: Submit. What does the watcher see?

arc.promise: Follow one request from browser to server, then say why the watcher now sees only noise, and what the padlock does and does not tell you.
arc.bridge_from_prior: No separate bridge for two minutes: the viewer already sees the padlock, and the promise leads straight into the build by naming the padlock as the result to explain.

sections.goal: the viewer can explain why plain traffic can be read by any device on the path
concepts: plain traffic is readable text (F1)
devices on the path that are neither end (F2)
can copy, nothing prevents it (F2)
sections.on_screen_change: Packets of readable text travel from browser to server; the watcher device on the path copies one and shows the same readable text.

sections.goal: the viewer can describe the three checks a browser makes on a server's certificate
concepts: browser asks server to identify itself (F5)
certificate and certificate authority (F6)
name matches, not expired, trusted issuer (F7)
sections.on_screen_change: A certificate card arrives at the browser; three ticks appear one at a time for name, date and issuer.

sections.goal: the viewer can explain how both ends end up with the same key while the watcher does not
concepts: key exchange: values sent in the open are not enough to work out the key (F9)
both ends hold the same key, the watcher does not (F10)
the key itself is never sent in the open (F9 caveat)
sections.on_screen_change: Browser and server each send a visible value across; the watcher copies both but gets no key; matching keys appear at the two ends only. No maths.

sections.goal: the viewer can describe how data is scrambled with the key and unscrambled at the far end, in both directions
concepts: encryption and decryption with a key (F4)
form data encrypted by browser, decrypted by server (F11)
watcher sees only scrambled data (F12)
replies protected the same way (F13)
HTTPS is HTTP inside TLS (F3)
sections.on_screen_change: The same readable form data turns into scrambled blocks at the browser, passes the watcher unchanged as noise, and turns readable again at the server.

sections.goal: the viewer can apply the three certificate checks to a new site whose certificate was issued for a different name
concepts: failed certificate check: browser warns, does not continue silently by default (F8)
overriding removes the identity check (F8 caveat)
sections.on_screen_change: The same request is sent to a site whose certificate card shows a different name; the name check turns red and the options appear.

sections.goal: the viewer can distinguish what the padlock shows from what it does not, and which two things to check before typing
concepts: padlock means encrypted and certificate accepted for that name (F14)
not proof of honesty or safety (F15)
no protection after arrival (F16)
read the exact site name and look for a warning (F17)
sections.on_screen_change: An address bar appears beside the padlock; two ticks are added (exact name, no warning); two 'does not show' labels are added beside it.

arc.payoff: Return to the opening form: same data, same network, same watcher, who now sees only scrambled noise, while the padlock closes. The viewer can answer the hook's question and says what they will check next time.

practice_ladder.what: The single request is walked through identity, key and scrambled data with the narrator doing each step.

practice_ladder.where: quiz after s4_scramble, answered in s5_check
practice_ladder.what: A new site with a certificate issued for a different name; the viewer decides what the browser should do before the answer appears.
The viewer applies the two-point check to a real form of their own after the video.

recall_moments.prompt: Remember the three certificate checks? The key only means something once the identity check has passed.
recall_moments.answer: Name matches, not expired, trusted issuer.

recall_moments.prompt: A site's certificate was issued for a different site name than the one in the address bar. What should the browser do?
options: Continue quietly, because the connection is still scrambled
Warn the user and not continue silently by default
Switch to the plain version of the site
recall_moments.answer: Warn the user and not continue silently by default
recall_moments.tempting_wrong: Continue quietly, because the connection is still scrambled. Scrambling alone does not say who holds the other end of the key; the identity check is what does, and overriding the warning removes it.

transfer_tasks: Before the next time you enter a password or card detail, read the site name in the address bar letter by letter and check that the browser shows no certificate warning, then decide whether to continue.

gagne.attention: arc.hook: the form submitted with a watcher on the path
gagne.recall_prior: arc.bridge_from_prior and audience.assumed_prior: the padlock the viewer already sees
gagne.present: arc.sections s1 to s4, then s6
gagne.guidance: strategy.signature_move and the worked steps in practice_ladder
gagne.practice: pacing.recall_moments: recall_prompt after s3_key, quiz after s4_scramble
gagne.feedback: the quiz answer card explains why the tempting option fails
gagne.assess: the quiz after s4_scramble; no further assessment in two minutes

merrill.problem_centred: one form submission with a watcher runs through every section
merrill.activation: the padlock the viewer already sees
merrill.demonstration: s2 to s4 show each step on the same request
merrill.application: quiz after s4_scramble, answered in s5_check
merrill.integration: s6_habit and transfer_tasks put the check into the viewer's own typing

mayer.coherence: one board, no decoration, no people
mayer.signalling: one loud change at a time, listed in each section's on_screen_change
mayer.redundancy: narration carries the explanation; on-screen text is labels only
mayer.contiguity: each label appears as the narration names the idea
mayer.segmenting: six short sections, one idea each
mayer.pre_training: each term is named only after it has been seen on screen

arcs.attention: the viewer is the person whose form is exposed
arcs.relevance: what they type at work and at home
arcs.confidence: one request, three steps, no maths
arcs.satisfaction: the payoff shows the watcher seeing only noise

framework_audit.bloom_path: understand -> understand -> understand -> understand -> apply -> analyze

flags: REST-TOO-SHORT: a rest section over 180 s cannot fit in a 120 s video; s6_habit is the only rest, at about 14 s.
Key agreement kept to the idea only (F9 caveat); no maths. Browser padlock designs differ and change (F14 caveat), so the picture should be generic.
The watcher can still see that a connection exists and usually which server (F12 caveat); not shown as hidden.
